extracted.intended_audience: grant writers and proposal development teams at colleges, universities, and nonprofit organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for selecting funding sources and preparing competitive grant proposals for institutional and program funding (primarily for higher-education and nonprofit contexts). Covers pre-proposal research, proposal structure, writing, budgeting, review, submission, and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match to funder's priorities and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacting a potential funding source, first determine if your application will fit their priorities and if your institution is an eligible applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether your request will meet the organization's goals for the next funding cycle; whether a preliminary proposal or concept paper is required; who is the most appropriate person to speak with; the amount available, typical award size, number of awards, and whether partial awards are made; and cycle deadlines. Use personal letter or telephone contact to clarify questions after reviewing the application package.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request and review the funder's application package
rubrics_metrics.description: Request the grant application package from each promising funding source and review materials that describe the organization's purpose, structure, funding priorities, proposal requirements and procedures, schedule and amount of awards, and special instructions and forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If questions remain after review, contact a representative. The more completely you understand a grant program, the better your chance of writing a winning proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research past grantees and external contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain more information about an organization, contact previous grant applicants (winners and losers) and individuals in other organizations or colleges who may have had dealings with pertinent funding organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for copies of past proposals and insights from people who write or read proposals regularly. Also contact members of charitable bodies, school boards, legislative staff, local civic and business leaders to explore their willingness to help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary planning and needs analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful proposals are a triumph of careful planning and preparation; take adequate time to analyze program needs and apply to the most promising sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughtful preliminary planning makes writing easier and the final proposal more competitive. Develop strong statement of need from compiled needs-analysis data and include supporting data in appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the funder's perspective / anticipate reviewer questions
rubrics_metrics.description: View the submission from the perspective of the funding organization by asking the kinds of questions that reviewers will ask.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical concerns include: Is the main idea clearly and logically presented? Does the project merit the amount requested? What distinguishes the proposed program from others? Is the content and style impressive? Are assurances given that the funds will be spent wisely?

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow requested format and include required pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the format requested by the funding agency or copy the format used in previous successful proposals. Include all required pieces and do not include extraneous or expensive-looking enclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the funding organization requires a specific format, it should take precedence. Extraneous materials may send the wrong message regarding cost concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: State program objectives as measurable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the program objectives in terms of measurable results that reflect important outcomes for students, faculty, the institution, and/or the community at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of program results that would make good newspaper stories. Use bulleted, hard-hitting objective statements highlighting the most important factor of interest to the sponsor (e.g., special populations served, targeted industry, economic development goals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how requested funds will enable objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a careful explanation of how the requested funds will enable your program to meet the program objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding organizations look for assurances that the funds they expend will result in positive outcomes; directly link budget items and activities to objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, concise, and audience-appropriate writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the use of obscure language and convoluted writing. Good proposals are clear; key ideas are presented concisely and are understandable to laypersons as well as experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to state the key concept of the idea underlying your proposal in one sentence. Avoid overly technical language that may alienate non-expert reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly complex or unfocused approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: If your proposal offers overly complex or too many alternative approaches, it may be judged as overly technical or lacking in focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose clear, focused, reasonable approaches rather than multiple competing alternatives that dilute the main idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate confidence and avoid hedging
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to demonstrate confidence in the approach, ideas, and outcomes. Avoid broadcasting self-doubt with 'ifs' and 'buts' and 'maybes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State what will be done; when in doubt, do not propose risky ventures. Present achievable, well-justified plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use data and evidence effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Data, especially in the form of numbers and graphs, help make a strong case. Data should come from reliable sources and present or support needs, timetables, specific evaluation plans, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, show the cost per student over several years to highlight return on investment. Include supporting data in appendices as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate broader value and external support
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong proposals show that the outcomes to be achieved will be of value to more than one group and include evidence that your program is supported by others, especially outside your institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include letters of support from those involved or affected by the program, evidence of outside volunteers, advisory panel evidence, and in-kind contributions of equipment, supplies, or staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid requesting inappropriate or historically inadequate funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Good proposals do not ask for funds for programs that should be getting regular funding from within your system nor do they ask for money to conduct a program that has been tried and proven inadequate by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funders look for innovative but reasonable projects that deal creatively with real issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include recognition opportunities for the funder
rubrics_metrics.description: Where practical, include some sincere form of recognition of the funder (e.g., naming, plaques, invitations, publicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate foundations or philanthropists often like acknowledgements such as facility naming, plaques, invitations to see the program, testimonial affairs, or media publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate personal contact with funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Know that funding decisions are sometimes made independent of the proposal process; funders provide funds to individuals and groups they know and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing replaces personal contact—funding is a people business. Personal contact, respect, and trust can compensate for limited proposal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a proposal development sign-off schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a proposal development sign-off schedule to manage the writing process, listing title, funding organization, writers/reviewers, and critical steps with sign-off spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single-sheet schedule helps coordinate writing, reviewing, typing, sign-off and mailing responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward planning of the writing timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing the time schedule, start with the final date the proposal will be mailed and plan backwards to establish preceding dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow adequate time for each step and for delays due to busy schedules, extra reviewer revisions, unexpected budget revisions, clerical tasks, and duplication. Share the timeline with all participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page contents and format
rubrics_metrics.description: A title page may contain: (1) proposal title, (2) funding organization name, (3) principal investigator's name, (4) project time span (start and end dates), (5) amount of funding requested, and (6) date of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check institutional business office for standard format; some funders require a specific format. A separate signature page may be used if preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract length and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract: The purpose, activities, and outcomes of the proposed project should be described in 150 to 300 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a preliminary draft of the abstract before the full proposal to clarify key ideas; share it with other writers/reviewers; revise after the full proposal is completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background subsection content
rubrics_metrics.description: Background subsection should present important information about the proposing institution, its mission, situation, and the particular problem or need being addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show institution's capacity by summarizing similar previous projects, measures of effectiveness, relationships with other organizations, and past uses of funds obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of problem/need strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The Statement of the Problem subsection should describe the need to be addressed; reviewers may retain or eliminate proposals based on this section during early review cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present strongest statement of problem/need with concise summary and supporting data in appendices; explain costs of not resolving the problem and expected benefits from the requested funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project objectives clarity and prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the specific intended outcomes of the proposed project clearly—objective statements should present the most important factor of interest to the sponsor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bulleted and possibly bold-typed objective statements to catch the sponsor's interest; make this subsection hard-hitting and solid in terms of valuable results and differences achievable only with sponsor's help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan of Action – Activities overview
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plan of Action should present a detailed explanation of procedures and activities to be conducted, giving an overview of how the project will start, operate, and be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List major steps or phases so it is clear what will be done and when objectives will be achieved; include an Activities subsection overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan of Action – Tasks detail and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Tasks subsection, present detailed descriptions of each activity and step; organize by phases, activities, and tasks and number each item so order and relatedness is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number task items and include the task numbers on the timeline schedule to help readers understand scheduling. Provide concrete task examples as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time Line/calendar of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a Time Line subsection containing a calendar of events with notes; use the outline of phases, activities, and tasks to place lines/symbols on a chart showing when each part begins and ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures or charts (e.g., Gantt-like) to visually show start/end points; present sample project time line when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff section: roles, responsibilities, and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide information on staff who will work on the project, including their roles, responsibilities, and qualifications; a table may show amount of time per month each staff person will spend over the project duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name persons who will fill positions and add a few words on their qualifications. A staff matrix is advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilities description
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the facilities (buildings, labs, classrooms) in which the program will operate and any features important to carrying out the project work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include floor plans or other drawings to clarify plans where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methods tied to objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in detail the methods to be used to evaluate outcomes or success of the program; evaluation discussion should be precise and separate from Methods earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation methods and measures should relate directly to objectives and indicate how degree of success will be measured. Plan evaluation as though findings will support a follow-up proposal; include copies of assessment instruments in an appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget: itemized and year-by-year breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: The budget section should identify each item of cost separately and may group items into categories (salaries, fees, tuition waivers, equipment, etc.). For multi-year projects prepare a total budget followed by a year-by-year breakdown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common budget formats or institutional standard forms; a sample budget format is illustrated in appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect costs and funder limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect costs for overhead and administration usually are not charged directly to a project; institutions have a standard indirect rate applied as a percentage of direct costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most funding organizations have limits on indirect costs they will pay—check with a funding agency representative to ensure your institution's indirect costs are within their guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity statement: resources and past achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a capacity section describing resources and past achievements of your institution/program to show ability to carry out the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the project will be conducted successfully and in a manner that makes the sponsor proud. Be confident and positive without sounding arrogant; provide supporting data with minimal self-congratulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resumes: consistent format and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Include resumes in an appendix to show staff are experienced and qualified; if a position will be filled upon funding, include credentials for the prospective hire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same resume format for all staff unless the funder stipulates a format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal and external review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the proposal reviewed by individuals within your institution and, where helpful, by individuals outside the institution from a non-educator perspective; use a reviewer checklist to focus comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect reviewer suggestions, review each one carefully, and make appropriate revisions. Don't be a slave to reviewers' suggestions but use them as a guide. Thank reviewers and notify them of results to encourage future help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission format, copies, and mailing procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a final typed copy (usually double-spaced with specified margins), number the pages, duplicate enough copies, reproduce on good quality paper, and bind appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use registered mail and keep the postal receipt as evidence of on-time submission. After delivery allow time for logging, then call to confirm arrival if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain orderly files and be prepared to supply additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to supply additional support and clarifying information if requested after review; maintain an orderly file of items related to project scope, capacity, fiscal issues, budget, and evidence of need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep supporting documents organized so they can be provided quickly upon request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request evaluative feedback after rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposal is not funded, request as much evaluative feedback as can be provided to help improve the next attempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feedback to strengthen future proposals and follow up with reviewers or funder contacts when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical details for approaching corporate/program funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Different corporations and foundations have stated preferences (geographic focus, program interests, application deadlines, initial contact method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow each funder's stated instructions: initial contact by letter or phone, number of proposal copies required, board meeting schedules, and any required preliminary concept papers or sponsor relationships (e.g., Hewlett-Packard requires an HP employee sponsor). Consult specific funder guidelines before applying.
